sceneHappening: A third visit, a call to examine yourselves, and a final blessing
summary: This will be Paul's third visit to Corinth. "Every word shall be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses." He said it before on the second visit and says it again now while absent: if he comes again, he will not spare those who sinned earlier or any others, since they seek proof that Christ speaks in him, who is not weak toward them but powerful among them. "For he was crucified through weakness, yet he lives through the power of God. For we also are weak in him, but we will live with him through the power of God toward you." Then he turns the question around: "Test yourselves, to see if you are in the faith. Test yourselves. Or don't you know as to yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you? unless indeed you are disqualified." He hopes they will know that he and his companions are not disqualified, and prays that they will do no wrong, not so that Paul will appear to pass the test, but so that they do what is right, even if he looks like he has failed. "For we can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth." He rejoices when they are strong and he is weak, and prays for their restoration. He writes this while absent so that when present he will not have to use severity, according to the authority which the Lord gave him for building up and not for tearing down. In closing: "Finally, brothers, rejoice! Be perfected. Be comforted. Be of the same mind. Live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you. Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the saints greet you. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all."
whySettingMatters: The rule about two or three witnesses comes from Deuteronomy 19:15 and was used in Jewish law and in the early church (Matthew 18:16). Paul uses it to say that his three visits are the three witnesses, a way of saying that the matter must be settled. The Corinthians have been asking for "proof" that Christ is speaking through Paul, and Paul gives the question back: the real test is whether they are in the faith, and the evidence that Christ is in them is the very life of the church that Paul founded. The statement that Christ "was crucified in weakness but lives by the power of God" sums up the whole letter's argument: weakness and power belong together in Christ and so in Paul. The closing blessing (13:14) is the fullest threefold statement in Paul's letters, naming the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, which is one reason it became a standard Christian benediction. The end of the letter also leaves some things uncertain: we do not know exactly how the visit went, though Acts 20:2-3 says Paul spent three months in Greece, and Romans, written during this time, is peaceful.

people.note: Plans a third visit and calls for self-examination.
Told to test themselves and to be restored.
Crucified in weakness, living by God's power.

questions: Paul gives the Corinthians' demand for proof back to them with "examine yourselves." What does that reverse?
"Crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God." How does that sentence organize the whole letter?
Paul wants restoration, not punishment. What does restoration look like when relationships have been strained?
The closing blessing names Father, Son, and Spirit. What does it say about what the church shares?
